paper_context.research_question: Is social and behavioral information available on Twitter sufficient for constructing a reliable weakly supervised classifier for political framing on the platform, and how do such models perform?
contribution_type: Methodological development of weakly supervised collective classification models for political framing on Twitter.
Empirical validation of the effectiveness of combining lexical and network-based behavioral features for frame prediction.
Creation and annotation of a dataset of U.S. Congressional tweets for political framing analysis, including proposed Twitter-specific frames.
Qualitative analysis demonstrating the utility of frame prediction for understanding political discourse and identifying political behaviors (e.g., aisle-crossing politicians).
main_claims: Weakly supervised collective classification models leveraging both lexical and network-based behavioral features can effectively predict political frames in Twitter discourse.

Combining behavioral features (temporal activity, retweets, follower networks) with lexical features significantly improves F1 scores for frame prediction, particularly in unsupervised settings (21.52 points increase over a lexical baseline).

The proposed models can be used to identify and analyze political framing patterns over time, across parties, and for individual politicians, including the identification of 'aisle-crossing' behavior.

Three new Twitter-specific frames (Factual, Promotion, Personal Sympathy and Support) are introduced and integrated into the framing analysis, adapting existing guidelines for the microblogging context.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Technical soundness and novelty of the proposed weakly supervised collective classification models (PSL framework) and feature engineering.

Rigour and comprehensiveness of the experimental evaluation, including baselines, metrics (F1 score, precision, recall for multilabel classification), and analysis of supervised vs. unsupervised settings.
Quality and utility of the collected and annotated Twitter dataset for political discourse analysis, including the appropriateness of the new Twitter-specific frames.
Effectiveness of integrating diverse feature types (lexical, temporal, network) for improved prediction performance.
Insightfulness and practical implications of the qualitative analysis of framing patterns and aisle-crossing politicians.
Reproducibility of results and availability of the dataset and methods.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The adapted Boydstun et al. annotation guidelines, with the addition of three Twitter-specific frames, are appropriate and sufficient for capturing political framing on Twitter.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The small seed set of keywords adapted from Boydstun et al. is a sufficient 'weak supervision' signal for the PSL models to learn frame predictions, especially in the unsupervised setting.

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the initial seed keywords are not sufficiently representative or comprehensive, the weak supervision could lead to biased or incomplete model learning, impacting the accuracy and generalizability of frame predictions, particularly in the unsupervised setting.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The temporal similarity heuristic (tweets occurring around the same time share similar frames) and network similarity heuristics (retweeting/following implies similar ideologies/frames) accurately capture meaningful behavioral dependencies for frame prediction.
supporting_evidence: We expect that the frames used the day of an event will be similar and change over time. (Section 4.3)

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these behavioral patterns do not consistently correlate with shared framing, the integration of these features might introduce noise or spurious correlations, potentially limiting the genuine performance improvement of the collective classification models.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 'aisle-crossing' behavior identified through voting records is sufficiently reflected in Twitter framing patterns to be detectable by the proposed models.
supporting_evidence: These are politicians who do not vote the same as the majority vote of their party (i.e., they vote the same as the opposing party). (Section 6)

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a logically structured argument for the effectiveness of weakly supervised collective classification, leveraging lexical and behavioral features, for political framing on Twitter. The paper progresses from defining the challenging task and introducing a novel dataset with adapted frames, through detailing the PSL-based methodology, to presenting empirical results and a qualitative analysis demonstrating practical utility. The core argument that combining diverse features significantly improves performance, especially in unsupervised settings, is well-supported by experimental data. However, the interpretation of inter-annotator agreement and the generalizability of some qualitative observations warrant closer scrutiny for full logical coherence.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Understanding political discourse on social media, specifically nuanced political framing on Twitter, is important but challenging due to dynamic language and short text length (Section 1).
P2: Traditional supervised methods are impractical for dynamic political discourse due to continuous data changes (Section 1, Section 5).
C1: Weakly supervised collective classification, leveraging social and behavioral information, can reliably predict political frames on Twitter (Section 1).
E1.1: A dataset of U.S. Congressional tweets is collected and annotated, adapting existing framing guidelines and introducing Twitter-specific frames (Section 3).
E1.2: A Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) framework is used to model dependencies between tweet frame predictions based on author interactions and behavioral similarity (Section 1, Section 4).

E1.3: PSL models incorporate language-based features (unigrams, bigrams, trigrams) and Twitter behavior-based features (temporal similarity, retweet patterns, follower networks) (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).
C2: Combining behavioral features with lexical features significantly improves F1 scores for frame prediction, particularly in unsupervised settings (Section 1, Section 5).
E2.1: Experimental results (Table 4, Table 6) show a 21.52 point increase in average unsupervised F1 score over a lexical baseline when combining features (Section 5).
E2.2: Detailed F1 scores per frame (Table 6) demonstrate Model 6 (combined features) generally outperforms other models in unsupervised settings (Section 5).
C3: The proposed models can be used for insightful qualitative analysis of political framing patterns and identification of 'aisle-crossing' politicians (Section 1, Section 6).
E3.1: Qualitative analysis shows distinct framing patterns for Democrats and Republicans on issues like ACA and terrorism (Figure 3, Section 6).
E3.2: Analysis of 'aisle-crossing' Republicans on ACA votes reveals their use of typically Democrat-associated frames (Figure 4a, Section 6).
E3.3: Observations for 'aisle-crossing' Democrats on terrorism votes suggest additional frames might indicate different voting behaviors, though based on a small scale (Figure 4b, Section 6).
C4: The PSL models are generalizable to other domains by adapting initial unigram keywords (Section 7).

concerns.title: Ambiguity in Inter-Annotator Agreement Interpretation
concerns.description: The inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa of 73.4%) is presented as 'proof of the difficulty of frame classification for tweets.' While it indicates task complexity, it does not inherently prove the *reliability* or *validity* of the adapted frames or annotation guidelines themselves. This logical leap could undermine confidence in the ground truth used for evaluation.
evidence: Section 3: 'We computed the inter-annotator agreement using Cohen’s Kappa statistic and have an agreement of 73.4%, which can be viewed as proof of the difficulty of frame classification for tweets.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify whether the Kappa score is considered acceptable for the task's complexity and discuss its implications for the reliability of the gold standard. Provide additional context or justification for the adapted frames and guidelines, perhaps with examples of difficult cases and how they were resolved.

concerns.title: Limited Generalizability of Aisle-Crossing Observations
concerns.description: The qualitative analysis of 'aisle-crossing' Democrats on terrorism votes is explicitly noted to be based on a 'small scale of these tweets.' This limits the robustness and generalizability of the specific findings for this group, potentially weakening the overall claim about the model's utility for identifying such behavior across all contexts.
evidence: Section 6: 'However, given the small scale of these tweets, we can also consider Frames 12 and 13 to show peaks for this example. This suggests that for aisle-crossing Democrats the use of additional frames not seen in their party might indicate potentially different voting behaviors.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Acknowledge this limitation more explicitly in the conclusion or discuss potential future work to gather more data for such sparse groups to strengthen the generalizability of these specific insights.

concerns.title: Justification for New Twitter-Specific Frames
concerns.description: While three new Twitter-specific frames are introduced, the justification for their selection and their distinctness from existing frames (beyond 'Other' being unused) could be more thoroughly elaborated. A deeper discussion on how these frames specifically capture microblogging nuances and how they were validated beyond inter-annotator agreement would strengthen the argument for their appropriateness.

Table 1: Lists the new frames with brief descriptions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more detailed rationale for why these specific frames are necessary for Twitter and how they differ from or complement the adapted Boydstun frames. Perhaps include examples of tweets that clearly demonstrate the unique utility of these new frames.

It supports the paper's premise that social information can be effective for political inference, even outperforming text-based models in some cases. The retrieved snippet specifically mentions 'friend features may be less susceptible to such data drift' and 'the friend-based distant model performs much better than the text-based model (.80 vs .56)' for political classification, which aligns with the current paper's findings on the utility of network-based behavioral features.

alternative_interpretations: The noted 'difficulty' in frame classification (73.4% Kappa) could alternatively be interpreted as an indication that the adapted Boydstun frames, even with additions, might not perfectly capture the nuances of Twitter discourse, or that the annotation guidelines themselves could benefit from further refinement for this specific platform.

The observed 'aisle-crossing' framing patterns, while insightful, might not always directly correlate with actual voting behavior or could be influenced by other factors not captured by the model, such as strategic communication rather than genuine ideological shift.

The choice of two issues (ACA and terrorism) for detailed qualitative analysis is justified by their frequency in the dataset, enhancing transparency in selection.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While components like weak supervision, collective classification (PSL), and the use of network features for political analysis exist in the literature (e.g., Culotta et al., 2016 for demographics, Johnson & Goldwasser, 2016 for stance), the specific combination of these elements for the nuanced task of *political framing* on Twitter, coupled with the introduction of Twitter-specific frames and the empirical validation of diverse feature types, represents a novel integration and application. The innovation lies in the synthesis and empirical demonstration for this particular, challenging task.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: The adapted framing guidelines and newly proposed Twitter-specific frames are robust and universally applicable to political discourse on the platform, beyond the U.S. Congressional context.
The weak supervision signal (initial unigram seed sets) is sufficiently representative and comprehensive to enable effective learning across all frames and issues, minimizing bias.
The behavioral heuristics (temporal activity, retweeting, follower networks) consistently and accurately reflect shared framing ideologies across diverse political actors and contexts.
The identified 'aisle-crossing' framing patterns are consistently predictive of actual voting behavior or significant ideological shifts, making the model a reliable tool for political analysis.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a weakly supervised collective classification framework utilizing Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) to predict political frames within U.S. Congressional tweets. The core methodological innovation lies in combining traditional lexical features (unigrams, bigrams, trigrams) with network-based behavioral features (temporal activity, retweet patterns, follower networks) to enhance frame prediction. Weak supervision is achieved through a small seed set of keywords. The evaluation demonstrates significant F1 score improvements, particularly in unsupervised settings, when integrating these diverse features. Furthermore, the paper applies the best-performing unsupervised model to conduct a qualitative analysis of framing patterns over time, across parties, and for identifying 'aisle-crossing' politicians. A new dataset of U.S. Congressional tweets is presented, along with an adaptation of existing framing guidelines and the introduction of three Twitter-specific frames.
logical_argument_graph: Political framing on Twitter is a challenging multilabel classification task due to short text and dynamic discourse.
Weakly supervised collective classification, specifically using PSL, can leverage dependencies between tweets and authors to address these challenges.
Lexical features (unigrams, bigrams, trigrams) provide content-based signals for frames.
Behavioral features (temporal similarity, retweet patterns, follower networks) capture social and temporal dependencies among politicians, hypothesized to correlate with shared framing.
PSL rules integrate these diverse features and dependencies, allowing for collective inference of frames.
A small seed set of keywords provides weak supervision, making the approach applicable to dynamic, unannotated data.
Experimental results (F1 scores) demonstrate that combining lexical and behavioral features significantly improves frame prediction, especially in unsupervised settings.
The trained models can be applied to large, unlabeled datasets to identify and analyze political framing patterns, including the detection of 'aisle-crossing' behavior.
Therefore, social and behavioral information on Twitter is sufficient for constructing a reliable weakly supervised classifier for political framing, and such models perform effectively.

strengths.title: Integrated Feature Set for Weak Supervision
strengths.description: The paper effectively integrates diverse feature types (lexical, temporal, network) within a Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) framework. This approach is robust for weakly supervised collective classification, particularly valuable for nuanced tasks like political framing where labeled data is scarce and contextual dependencies are crucial.
evidence: Our global probabilistic models show that by combining both lexical features of tweets and network-based behavioral features of Twitter, we are able to increase the average, unsupervised F1 score by 21.52 points over a lexical baseline alone. (Abstract)

We approach this task using a weakly supervised collective classification approach which leverages the dependencies between tweet frame predictions based on the interactions between their authors. (Section 1)

We compile these structural dependencies into a graphical model using Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL)... PSL combines these aspects declaratively by specifying high level rules over a relational representation of tweet features. (Section 1)

strengths.title: Comprehensive Evaluation Settings

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a meaningful incremental contribution by extending established political framing analysis techniques and computational methods to the challenging domain of Twitter political discourse. It refines existing paradigms by adapting the Boydstun et al. framing codebook for microblogging, introducing Twitter-specific frames, and reorganizing feature integration within a Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) framework. The core contribution lies in demonstrating that combining lexical, temporal, and network-based behavioral features, under a weakly supervised collective classification approach, significantly improves frame prediction, particularly in unsupervised settings. This approach offers a practical extension for analyzing nuanced political communication and identifying specific political behaviors like 'aisle-crossing' politicians, building upon existing work in distant supervision and social network analysis for political inference.
logical_argument_graph: Understanding political discourse on social media is crucial, but automated analysis of nuanced tasks like political framing on Twitter is difficult due to dynamic language and the cost of direct supervision (Premise 1).

Twitter provides rich social and behavioral information (temporal activity, retweets, follower networks) that can be leveraged as weak supervision signals, offering an alternative to direct supervision (Premise 2).

Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) is a suitable methodological framework for declaratively combining diverse features and dependencies within a weakly supervised collective classification setting (Premise 3).

Existing political framing guidelines (Boydstun et al.) can be adapted for Twitter, and new Twitter-specific frames are necessary to capture the unique aspects of microblogging. A dataset of U.S. Congressional tweets can be collected and annotated to support this (Premise 4).

Therefore, the authors propose developing PSL models that integrate lexical features (unigrams, bigrams, trigrams) with behavioral features (temporal similarity, retweet patterns, follower networks) using a small seed set of keywords for weak supervision (Action).
Experimental evaluation in both supervised and unsupervised settings, using F1 score, will assess the effectiveness of these models (Experiment).

The experiments demonstrate that combining lexical and behavioral features significantly improves F1 scores for frame prediction, especially in unsupervised settings (21.52 points increase over a lexical baseline), validating the utility of the combined approach (Result 1, Claim C2).

Furthermore, the proposed models can be effectively used for qualitative analysis of political framing patterns over time, across parties, and for individual politicians, including the identification of 'aisle-crossing' behavior, providing practical insights into political dynamics (Result 2, Claim C3).

In conclusion, weakly supervised collective classification leveraging combined lexical and behavioral features is an effective and valuable approach for political framing on Twitter, offering a robust tool for political discourse analysis (Conclusion).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a novel approach to political framing prediction on Twitter by integrating weakly supervised collective classification within a Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) framework. Its core contribution lies in demonstrating that a combination of lexical features with network-based behavioral features (temporal activity, retweets, follower networks) can significantly improve F1 scores for this complex, multilabel task, particularly in unsupervised settings. The paper also introduces three new Twitter-specific frames, adapting existing political framing theory (Boydstun et al.) to the microblogging context. Finally, it explores the practical utility of its best-performing model through a qualitative analysis of framing patterns across parties and for identifying 'aisle-crossing' politicians, suggesting a new avenue for political discourse analysis. The paper's reasoning is that the dynamic and short-text nature of Twitter data makes traditional supervised learning difficult for nuanced tasks like framing, thus necessitating a weakly supervised approach that can leverage rich relational and behavioral signals available on the platform.
logical_argument_graph: Political discourse on social media, especially Twitter, requires automated analysis tools due to its dynamic nature and influence.
Political framing is a nuanced analysis task, and Twitter presents challenges due to short text and evolving language.
Direct supervision for framing on Twitter is impractical due to data dynamics.

Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) is used to model dependencies between tweet frame predictions based on author interactions (temporal similarity, retweets, follower networks) and lexical features.
Existing framing guidelines (Boydstun et al.) are adapted for Twitter, and three new Twitter-specific frames are introduced to better capture microblogging nuances.

The best-performing unsupervised model is applied to analyze framing patterns over time, by party, and for individual politicians.
This qualitative analysis provides insights into political discourse and suggests a method for identifying 'aisle-crossing' politicians based on their framing patterns.

Thus, social and behavioral information on Twitter is sufficient for constructing a reliable weakly supervised classifier for political framing, and these models offer valuable analytical capabilities.

concerns.title: Robustness of Weak Supervision and Feature Utility Nuances

This raises questions about the model's ability to learn effectively for frames with sparse or ambiguous seed signals.

prior_stage_inputs: The manuscript presents a logically structured argument for the effectiveness of weakly supervised collective classification, leveraging lexical and behavioral features, for political framing on Twitter. The paper progresses from defining the challenging task and introducing a novel dataset with adapted frames, through detailing the PSL-based methodology, to presenting empirical results and a qualitative analysis demonstrating practical utility. The core argument that combining diverse features significantly improves performance, especially in unsupervised settings, is well-supported by experimental data. However, the interpretation of inter-annotator agreement and the generalizability of some qualitative observations warrant closer scrutiny for full logical coherence.

The paper introduces a weakly supervised collective classification framework utilizing Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) to predict political frames within U.S. Congressional tweets. The core methodological innovation lies in combining traditional lexical features (unigrams, bigrams, trigrams) with network-based behavioral features (temporal activity, retweet patterns, follower networks) to enhance frame prediction. Weak supervision is achieved through a small seed set of keywords. The evaluation demonstrates significant F1 score improvements, particularly in unsupervised settings, when integrating these diverse features. Furthermore, the paper applies the best-performing unsupervised model to conduct a qualitative analysis of framing patterns over time, across parties, and for identifying 'aisle-crossing' politicians. A new dataset of U.S. Congressional tweets is presented, along with an adaptation of existing framing guidelines and the introduction of three Twitter-specific frames.

The manuscript presents a meaningful incremental contribution by extending established political framing analysis techniques and computational methods to the challenging domain of Twitter political discourse. It refines existing paradigms by adapting the Boydstun et al. framing codebook for microblogging, introducing Twitter-specific frames, and reorganizing feature integration within a Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) framework. The core contribution lies in demonstrating that combining lexical, temporal, and network-based behavioral features, under a weakly supervised collective classification approach, significantly improves frame prediction, particularly in unsupervised settings. This approach offers a practical extension for analyzing nuanced political communication and identifying specific political behaviors like 'aisle-crossing' politicians, building upon existing work in distant supervision and social network analysis for political inference.

The manuscript proposes a novel approach to political framing prediction on Twitter by integrating weakly supervised collective classification within a Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) framework. Its core contribution lies in demonstrating that a combination of lexical features with network-based behavioral features (temporal activity, retweets, follower networks) can significantly improve F1 scores for this complex, multilabel task, particularly in unsupervised settings. The paper also introduces three new Twitter-specific frames, adapting existing political framing theory (Boydstun et al.) to the microblogging context. Finally, it explores the practical utility of its best-performing model through a qualitative analysis of framing patterns across parties and for identifying 'aisle-crossing' politicians, suggesting a new avenue for political discourse analysis. The paper's reasoning is that the dynamic and short-text nature of Twitter data makes traditional supervised learning difficult for nuanced tasks like framing, thus necessitating a weakly supervised approach that can leverage rich relational and behavioral signals available on the platform.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper claims that weakly supervised collective classification models, by integrating both lexical and network-based behavioral features, can effectively predict political frames on Twitter, particularly showing significant F1 score improvements in unsupervised settings. This core claim is strongly supported by the quantitative experimental results presented in Tables 4 and 6, which demonstrate a substantial increase in F1 scores when combining features, especially in the unsupervised context. The introduction of three new Twitter-specific frames is a factual methodological step, well-documented in the text and Table 1. However, the claim regarding the utility of these models for definitively identifying 'aisle-crossing' behavior is partially supported; while the qualitative analysis provides insightful patterns and suggestions, the evidence is observational and explicitly noted to be on a 'small scale' for some groups, lacking rigorous quantitative validation for reliable identification. The paper's reasoning for leveraging weak supervision and diverse features in the dynamic Twitter environment is sound, and the empirical results largely corroborate the benefits of this approach, aligning with prior work on distant supervision and network features in political classification.
logical_argument_graph: Political discourse on Twitter is dynamic and nuanced, making traditional supervised framing analysis difficult (Section 1).
Weakly supervised collective classification, leveraging social and behavioral information, can address this challenge (Section 1).
A dataset of U.S. Congressional tweets is collected and annotated, adapting existing framing guidelines and introducing three Twitter-specific frames (Section 3).

Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) is used to model dependencies between tweet frame predictions, incorporating lexical features (unigrams, bigrams, trigrams) and behavioral features (temporal activity, retweets, follower networks) (Section 4).

The best-performing unsupervised model is applied to analyze framing patterns over time, across parties, and for individual politicians (Section 6).
This qualitative analysis provides insights into political discourse and suggests potential for identifying 'aisle-crossing' politicians based on their framing patterns (Section 6, Figures 3, 4).

concerns.title: Overstated Reliability for Aisle-Crossing Identification
concerns.description: While the qualitative analysis effectively demonstrates the *utility* of the model for exploring framing patterns related to 'aisle-crossing' behavior, the claim regarding its *identification* and *reliability* is overstated. The analysis is observational and explicitly notes limitations (e.g., 'small scale of these tweets' for Democrats), lacking quantitative validation for robust identification.

concerns.title: Nuanced Utility of Individual Behavioral Features
concerns.description: Claim C2 states significant improvement from combined features, which is true overall. However, the paper's own analysis in Section 5 highlights that certain individual behavioral features (e.g., bigrams, retweets) show less utility or even decrease F1 scores for specific frames in unsupervised settings. This nuance suggests that the 'combination' is not uniformly beneficial across all components or frames, and the blanket claim of 'significantly improves' could be refined.

This suggests that bigrams may not be as useful as trigrams in an unsupervised setting. Finally, in Model 5, which adds retweet behaviors, we notice that 5 of the frames decrease in F1 score and 11 of the frames have the same score as the previous model. These results suggest that retweet behaviors are not as useful as the follower network relationships in an unsupervised setting. (Section 5)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Refine the language around the 'significant improvement' to acknowledge the varying utility of individual features and discuss the specific conditions or frames where certain features are less effective. This would add precision to the claim.

Both papers demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging social network information for inferring political attributes.

The behavioral heuristics (temporal activity, retweets, follower networks) consistently and strongly correlate with shared political framing, making them reliable signals for collective classification.

Reviewers agree that the models show practical utility for analyzing political framing patterns over time, across parties, and for exploring 'aisle-crossing' behavior (Claim C3), although the reliability of definitive 'identification' is debated.

The creation of a new dataset of U.S. Congressional tweets, the adaptation of established framing guidelines, and the introduction of three Twitter-specific frames (Claim C4) are recognized as valuable contributions.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: n doubt, consider the scope described in ARR CFP and any relevant conferences (e.g. for October 2024 cycle the NAACL CFP specifies the special theme “NLP in a Multicultural World”. Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
